The bill

Most of the spend is already on closed models.

Menlo Ventures put enterprise spend on foundation-model APIs at $12.5 billion in 2025, inside $37 billion of enterprise generative-AI spend. In its mid-2025 update the same firm had API spend at $8.4 billion, up from $3.5 billion in November 2024. Provider share of that 2025 spend: Anthropic 40%, OpenAI 27%, Google 21%. Open-source models were 13% of production workloads at mid-year. Sources: State of Generative AI in the Enterprise, December 2025 and the mid-year update.

The FinOps Foundation’s 2026 report says 98% of practitioners now manage AI spend, up from 31% two years earlier, and that AI cost management is the skill teams most want to build. data.finops.org. The size of the cost-optimization tooling market itself is not a figure we found a credible source for, so it is not quoted here.

Four levers

Caching, batch, compression, and a local tier.

Each lever is real only where the workload fits. The audit says which calls are candidates. It does not apply a market-wide percentage to your bill.

01

Hybrid routing

Repetitive calls can run on hardware you own. Hard calls stay with the cloud model you already pay for. Quality is checked on your evals before traffic moves.

Hybrid routing
02

Prompt caching

Anthropic documents cache reads at 0.1× input. OpenAI’s cache discount is not cited here, because published figures conflict. Structuring a prompt for a cache hit is audit work.

Prompt caching
03

Batch API

Anthropic and OpenAI document a 50% batch discount, and it can stack with caching. Calls that can wait are the candidates. Calls that cannot wait are not.

Batch API
04

Prompt compression

LLMLingua reports up to 20× compression with about a 1.5-point drop on the datasets it tested. That is Microsoft’s paper, not a Boole result, and it is not every workload.

Prompt compression

Why hardware you own

A fixed cost, and a boundary around the data.

Cloud gateways route among cloud models. They do not put the cheap tier on a machine in your office. An on-prem box has a fixed cost and a low marginal cost per token. The break-even is your volume against that fixed cost. We calculate it in the audit. We do not print a universal saving.

Sensitive calls can stay on hardware you control. A prompt that never leaves the building is a different path from a prompt sent to a provider API. That is not a HIPAA determination, and it is not a claim that model downloads never touch the network. Weights still come from somewhere the first time.

The only speed Boole has measured is the browser demo: 12.3 tok/s, SmolLM2-135M Instruct Q4_K_M, 64 tokens, about 5187 ms, 4-core Xeon, WebAssembly, one thread, no GPU layers. A 20B model at 200 tok/s remains a goal. Server throughput is not claimed until it is measured.

Published research

Other people’s benchmarks, with the range.

RouteLLM (ICLR 2025) reports up to 3.66× cost savings on MT-Bench at 95% of GPT-4 quality, and only 1.41× on MMLU and 1.49× on GSM8K. The range is the result. arxiv.org/html/2406.18665v3. It is not a Boole deployment.

LLMLingua (Microsoft) reports up to 20× prompt compression with about a 1.5-point performance drop on the datasets it tested. arxiv.org/abs/2310.05736. Results depend on the workload. “Up to” is the authors’ best case, not a typical bill.

Questions

Answered up front.

Do you publish a savings percentage?

No. Boole will not publish a savings percentage until a real customer result exists, and only with their written permission. Published research is cited separately, with the benchmark and the range. Your result depends on your workload.

Will you replace our model provider?

No. The hard calls stay in the cloud, with the provider you already use. Menlo Ventures reported that 11% of teams changed model provider in the year before its mid-2025 update. The audit looks for repetitive calls that can move onto hardware you own, after your own evals pass.

What does the Token Cost Audit include?

The Token Cost Audit from Boole AI, Inc. includes a spend breakdown by endpoint and model; a list of caching, batch, and trimming candidates; a list of calls that could move to a local model, with quality tested on a sample; an on-prem break-even calculation from your volumes; and an implementation quote. Pricing is scoped per engagement. Boole does not publish a savings percentage. Whether any traffic should move depends on your workload and your own evals.

What about implementation and a managed plan?

Those are not priced on this site. Email hello@booleinference.com and we will scope them. The audit includes an implementation quote. It does not include the implementation itself.

What speed has Boole measured?

One number: 12.3 tok/s for SmolLM2-135M Instruct Q4_K_M, 64 tokens, about 5187 ms, on a 4-core Xeon CPU in WebAssembly, one thread, no GPU layers. That is the browser demo, not a server. A 20-billion-parameter model at 200 tok/s is a roadmap goal, not a measurement.

Where does a prompt go?

A call that stays in the cloud goes to that provider, as it does today. A call moved to hardware you own is generated from a local GGUF file. The Boole CLI still contacts Hugging Face to resolve a model file name, and it downloads weights that are not cached. This is not a security certification and not a HIPAA determination.
